Flathead sole (Hippoglossoides elassodon) is a commercially important pleuronectid inhabiting the North Pacific Ocean, where field surveys have documented substantial sexual dimorphism in ultimate size. Based on extensive trawl data and otolith-based growth analyses, females achieve a considerably larger maximum total length of 52 centimeters [Li = 52 centimeters], whereas males rarely surpass 49 centimeters [Li = 49 centimeters], a pattern attributed to differential energetic allocation during the reproductive season. This disparity in somatic growth is mirrored in the species' reproductive biology, with females beginning gonadal maturation at a length of 32.9 centimeters [Lp = 32.9 centimeters]. The corresponding body mass at this pubertal transition, derived from length-weight regressions fitted to local populations, averages approximately 349 grams [Wwp = approximately 349 grams]. These size thresholds underscore the importance of reaching a critical body dimension before the onset of vitellogenesis and gamete production.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified through histological examination of ovaries from spawning adults captured during the spring bloom. At the prevailing bottom temperature of 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 9% [GSI = 9%]. The index shows negligible variation between years in stable thermal regimes, suggesting that temperature plays a permissive rather than directly limiting role in gametogenic investment at this stock. Females are thought to produce a single batch of eggs annually.

Larval development begins with the release of pelagic, yolk-sac larvae following hatching, a stage characterized by complete reliance on endogenous reserves. The individual wet weight at birth, calculated from the average egg diameter of 0.92 millimeters using the volume of a sphere, corresponds to approximately 0.0004 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0004 grams]. This minute starting mass, less than half a milligram, necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding; first-feeding larvae begin consuming suitable zooplankton within days of mouth opening. Survivorship through the yolk-sac stage is strongly temperature-dependent, with food availability in the water column dictating the success of the trophic switch. The chorion, thin and transparent in this species, offers minimal physical protection but facilitates efficient gas exchange during embryogenesis.

Females reach an asymptotic body mass of approximately 1400 grams [Wwi = approximately 1400 grams], a value derived from local length-weight regressions, reflecting the high productivity of the benthic feeding grounds characteristically occupied by this flatfish. Males, owing to their smaller asymptotic length, typically reach a correspondingly lower maximum body weight that rarely exceeds 900 grams. Growth rates are highest during the first few years of life, after which somatic expansion slows markedly as resources are increasingly directed toward reproduction. The species exhibits a typical life span, under the cool temperature regime of 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C], of approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years], placing it among the longer-lived members of its genus.

Longevity in this species, recorded as a maximum of nearly 27 years [am = nearly 27 years], is facilitated by the cold, stable thermal habitat which depresses metabolic rates throughout ontogeny at a temperature of 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C]. The full life cycle, from fertilized egg to natural death, thus unfolds over a period roughly equivalent to twenty-seven years [am = twenty-seven years] when evaluated at a sustained temperature of 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C]. This extended lifespan allows multiple reproductive opportunities, offsetting the relatively low annual fecundity characteristic of the pleuronectid lineage. Female fecundity scales positively with body size, reinforcing the selective advantage of reaching the asymptotic length of 52 centimeters [Li = 52 centimeters]. The interplay between slow maturation, substantial asymptotic size, and protracted reproductive tenure defines the species' demographic profile in the Gulf of Alaska.
